passage: Behind the village school, a big boy grabbed Arnab's marbles. "Give me the blue one, or I'll push you in the ditch." Arnab's legs went wobbly. Then Pradeep ran up and stood right beside him, shoulder to shoulder. "Leave him alone," Pradeep said. His voice shook a little, but he did not move. The big boy snorted and dropped the marbles. Pradeep picked them up. "Come on. Let's tell Sir." They walked to the staff room together. Arnab held his marbles tight and felt tall. At lunch, he saved Pradeep a place beside him.

qa.q: What did the big boy threaten?
qa.a: He threatened to push Arnab in the ditch unless he gave him the blue marble.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when Pradeep stood beside him?
qa.a: He felt brave and cared for; his wobbly legs steadied and he felt tall.

qa.q: What did the two boys do that was wise after the big boy left?
qa.a: They went together to tell Sir, instead of dealing with it alone or fighting.

qa.q: What is it like for Pradeep to stand up to the big boy?
qa.a: He is scared too, since his voice shook, but he feels loyal enough to his friend to stay.

grounding: A young boy's friend stands beside him against a bully and says leave him alone, and they go to a teacher together.

passage: In the school yard in Madrid, an older boy snatched Diego's snack bag. "Mine now." Diego's eyes filled. He didn't know what to do. Rania marched over and stood next to him. "Leave him alone! Give it back." The older boy laughed, but Rania didn't move. She took Diego's hand. "We're telling Señora López." They went to her together. Señora López got the snack bag back and talked to the older boy. Later, when a small girl dropped her ball near the older boys, Diego walked over and stood beside her.

qa.q: Who got Diego's snack bag back?
qa.a: Señora López got the snack bag back.

qa.q: How did Diego feel when Rania stood next to him?
qa.a: He felt braver and cared for, no longer alone and unsure what to do.

qa.q: What did Diego learn from Rania, based on what he did later?
qa.a: He learned to stand beside someone smaller, so he walked over to the girl who dropped her ball.

qa.q: How might Rania feel holding Diego's hand?
qa.a: She probably feels protective and a bit nervous but determined to help her friend. 🙂

grounding: A young boy's friend stands beside him against an older child and they go to a teacher, and he later stands up for someone else.

passage:
"Varun, what was that crash?"
"Nothing, Papa."
Yusuf came in. The blue vase lay in pieces by the shoe rack.
"Who did this?"
"Moti did it. He wagged his tail."
Moti was asleep on the balcony. Varun's tummy felt heavy, like a stone. He stared at his feet.
Yusuf sat on the floor. "Varun, tell me the truth. I will not shout."
"I was throwing my ball," Varun whispered. "I wish it didn't break."
"Thank you for telling me. That was honest. Now, let's sweep it up carefully."

qa.q: Where was Moti when the vase broke?
qa.a: Moti was asleep on the balcony.

qa.q: How did Varun feel after he blamed Moti?
qa.a: He felt guilty and heavy, like a stone in his tummy, and wished the vase hadn't broken.

qa.q: What did Yusuf say that made it easier for Varun to tell the truth?
qa.a: He promised not to shout, then thanked Varun for being honest and asked him to help sweep up.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel seeing Varun stare at his feet?
qa.a: He may feel disappointed about the vase but understanding, seeing a scared child wishing it undone.

grounding: A young boy breaks a vase and blames the dog, feels guilty, and his parent invites the truth without shouting and thanks him.

passage:
Note from Sangeeta, Sahil's amma, in the family notebook.
At Nani's house today, Sahil knocked her brass vase off the shelf while chasing a balloon. It dented. When Nani asked, he said, "Tommy did it," looking at Nani's old dog. He could not look at us and he kept rubbing his tummy. I sat down with him and said, "Tell me the truth. I will not shout." He cried, "I did it. I wish it was not broken." I thanked him for being honest. He helped Nani polish the dent. He slept well tonight.

qa.q: What was Sahil chasing when the vase fell?
qa.a: Sahil was chasing a balloon.

qa.q: What does Sahil rubbing his tummy suggest?
qa.a: He felt guilty and uneasy about the lie, with a heavy feeling inside, and wished it could be undone.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta do that helped Sahil be honest?
qa.a: She sat with him, promised not to shout, and thanked him when he told the truth.

qa.q: How might Nani see Sahil helping polish the dent?
qa.a: She may feel touched that he owned up and tried to make it right. 🤍

grounding: A young boy dents a vase and blames a dog, feels guilty, and his mother invites the truth without shouting and thanks him.

passage:
"Sarita, why is your school book torn?"
"I don't know, Amma. A boy did it."
"Which boy?"
Sarita twisted her frock. "A... new boy."
Lakshmi knelt down. "You're shaking. Are you scared I'll shout?"
Sarita nodded. "Last time you shouted so loud."
Lakshmi was quiet. "I did. I'm sorry. I don't want you to be scared to tell me things. In this house, truth is safe. What happened?"
"I pulled it from the shelf and it ripped."
"Thank you. We'll tape it together."

qa.q: What had happened to Sarita's school book?
qa.a: It was torn; she pulled it from the shelf and it ripped.

qa.q: Why did Sarita blame a new boy?
qa.a: She was scared her Amma would shout loudly again, and the fear was bigger than wanting to be honest.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi change to make truth feel safe?
qa.a: She noticed Sarita's fear, apologised for shouting last time, said truth is safe at home and responded calmly.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel when Sarita says "Last time you shouted so loud"?
qa.a: She may feel a pang of guilt and realise her shouting is teaching Sarita to hide things.

grounding: A young girl lies because she fears being shouted at, and her mother makes the truth feel safe.

passage:
From Aadhya's class teacher, to her mother, Kalyani.
Today Aadhya spilt green paint on her new white uniform. When I asked, she said Meera did it, though I saw it happen. Then she went pale and whispered, "Please don't tell Mummy. She'll scold me so much." I told her accidents are okay and she is not in trouble with me. We washed it together. When I stopped asking who did it and said she was safe, she said, "It was me." I'm writing so we can both make telling the truth feel safe for her.

qa.q: What did Aadhya spill on her uniform?
qa.a: She spilt green paint on her new white uniform.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya blame Meera?
qa.a: She was afraid of being scolded at home, and the fear was bigger than her wish to be honest.

qa.q: What helped Aadhya finally say "It was me"?
qa.a: The teacher said accidents are okay and that she was safe, which took away the fear of punishment.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel reading this note?
qa.a: She may feel sad that Aadhya is so scared of her scolding, and want to make it safer to tell the truth at home.

grounding: A young girl lies about a paint spill because she fears being scolded, and admits it once the teacher makes it safe.

passage: The chocolate wrapper was on the sofa in their Pune flat. Dhruv held it up. "Disha, did you eat the chocolate before dinner?" Disha's cheeks went hot. Last week she had lied about the biscuits. "No, Papa. Really. I didn't." Dhruv looked at her face for a long moment. Then he nodded. "Okay. I believe you." Later they found Dadaji in the kitchen with chocolate on his moustache. Disha giggled. Then she hugged Papa's leg. "I'll always tell you the truth," she said. "Even about biscuits."

qa.q: Where did Dhruv find the chocolate wrapper?
qa.a: He found it on the sofa in their Pune flat.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when Papa said "I believe you"?
qa.a: She felt respected and trusted, and it made her want to earn that trust by always telling the truth.

qa.q: Which choice of Dhruv's helped Disha value honesty?
qa.a: He believed her even though she had lied last week, so honesty felt like a gift instead of a risk.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel when Disha hugs his leg?
qa.a: He probably feels touched and glad he trusted her. 😊

grounding: A parent believes his daughter even though she once lied, and she feels respected and wants to earn that trust.

passage:
"Akash, did you draw on the wall?"
"No, Papa."
Nitin crouched and looked at the blue lines by the door. "Last month you said no about the cupboard, and it was you."
"I know. But this time it's true."
"Hmm." Nitin looked at Akash for a long time. "Okay. I believe you."
Akash's face lit up. "Really?"
"Really."
That evening, his little cousin Pinky walked past with a blue crayon. Nitin laughed.
"See, Papa?"
"I see. Thank you for telling me the truth."
Akash stood up straight. "I'm going to keep being true."

qa.q: What colour were the lines on the wall?
qa.a: The lines by the door were blue.

qa.q: What does Akash standing up straight suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt proud and respected, trusted by his father, and eager to keep earning that trust.

qa.q: Why was it a risk for Nitin to believe Akash, and why was it worth it?
qa.a: Akash had lied before, but believing him showed that honesty is noticed and valued, which makes Akash want to stay truthful.

qa.q: What would change if Nitin had refused to believe Akash?
qa.a: Akash might feel that telling the truth was pointless, since he would be blamed anyway.

grounding: A father believes his son's denial despite a past lie, and the boy feels respected and wants to stay honest.

passage: In the little school by the paddy fields, Bosco's red crayon went missing. "Francis took it, Miss!" Bosco said, pointing. Francis's mouth fell open. Bosco was his friend. They shared a bench. Francis felt hot, hurt and all muddled. "I didn't!" His voice cracked. Trisha Miss came over. Francis took a breath. "Miss, I didn't take it. I was drawing with my green one." Trisha Miss looked in Bosco's pencil box. The red crayon was under the ruler. Bosco went pink. "Sorry, Francis." Francis nodded slowly. He did not share his crayons that afternoon.

qa.q: Where was the red crayon found?
qa.a: It was in Bosco's pencil box, under the ruler.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when Bosco blamed him?
qa.a: He felt angry, hurt and confused, because Bosco was his friend and it wasn't true.

qa.q: What did Francis do that was wise?
qa.a: He calmly told Trisha Miss what really happened instead of shouting back or hitting.

qa.q: How might Bosco feel when the crayon is found?
qa.a: He probably feels embarrassed and guilty, going pink as he says sorry.

grounding: A young boy is falsely accused by his friend of taking a crayon, feels hurt and confused, and tells the teacher what really happened.

passage: In a kindergarten in Lagos, Chidi's orange crayon disappeared. "Sami took my crayon!" Chidi told Mrs Okafor. Sami froze. He and Chidi played together every day. His tummy flipped with anger and hurt. Why would Chidi say that? Sami went to Mrs Okafor. "I didn't take it. I was at the sand table." Mrs Okafor checked. The crayon had rolled under Chidi's chair. Chidi mumbled, "Sorry. I thought you did." Sami folded his arms. "You said I did it." The next day Chidi brought him a mango slice and said sorry again. Sami let him sit beside him.

qa.q: Where had the orange crayon rolled?
qa.a: It had rolled under Chidi's chair.

qa.q: Why did Sami's tummy flip?
qa.a: He felt angry, hurt and confused that his friend Chidi would blame him for something he didn't do.

qa.q: What helped the friendship begin to recover?
qa.a: Chidi said sorry twice and brought a mango slice, showing he meant it, and Sami chose to let him sit beside him.

qa.q: How might Chidi feel when Sami folds his arms?
qa.a: Chidi may feel ashamed and worried he has hurt the friendship, which is why Chidi tries again the next day.

grounding: A young boy's friend wrongly says he took a crayon; he feels hurt, tells the teacher the truth, and the friendship recovers after a real sorry.

passage:
Note from Vidya's teacher, for home.
At circle time, Vidya told Sabina, "I have a real dinosaur at home. He sleeps under my bed and eats bananas." Sabina's eyes went round. Vidya looked very sure, even a little worried he might be hungry. I said, "What a fun story! Is it real or pretend?" Vidya thought hard. "Pretend... but a little bit real." Then the whole circle drew banana-eating dinosaurs. 🦕 You may hear more about him at dinner!

qa.q: What did Vidya say her dinosaur eats?
qa.a: She said he eats bananas.

qa.q: What does Vidya's worry about the dinosaur being hungry suggest?
qa.a: She half believed her own story; she felt playful and a little unsure where pretend ended and real began.

qa.q: Why was asking "real or pretend?" a wise choice?
qa.a: It enjoyed her imagination while gently helping her tell story from fact, without calling it a lie.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Vidya's dinosaur story?
qa.a: Sabina seems amazed and excited, with round eyes, and enjoys the story.

grounding: A young girl tells an imaginative story about a dinosaur at home, and a teacher enjoys it and asks whether it is real or pretend.

passage: At the village shop, Hemant leaned on the counter. "Yusuf Chacha, there's a dinosaur living in our cowshed. It's bigger than the buffalo." Yusuf Chacha raised his eyebrows. "A dinosaur! What colour?" "Green. With spikes." Hemant looked towards the cowshed as if checking. His mother frowned. "Hemant, don't tell lies." Hemant's face fell. Yusuf Chacha winked at him. "What a fun story. Is it real or pretend?" Hemant grinned. "Pretend. But it's a good one." "The best one I heard today," said Yusuf Chacha, and gave him a toffee.

qa.q: Where did Hemant say the dinosaur lived?
qa.a: He said it was in the cowshed.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when his mother said "don't tell lies"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and confused, because to him it was a playful story, not a lie.

qa.q: What did Yusuf Chacha do differently from Hemant's mother?
qa.a: He enjoyed the story and asked whether it was real or pretend, so Hemant could say it was pretend without shame.

qa.q: Why might Hemant's mother react differently from Yusuf Chacha?
qa.a: She may worry that stories will turn into lying, so she treats it as deceit rather than imagination.

grounding: A young boy tells a pretend story about a dinosaur, and an adult enjoys it and asks if it is real or pretend instead of calling it a lie.

passage: At the international school in Osaka, Kaito-sensei collected the counting sheets. Paulo had none. "Paulo, where's yours?" Paulo looked at the floor. "My mummy said I don't need to do it." He felt clever, then his hands went sweaty. Kaito-sensei nodded calmly. "Okay. I'll send her a quick message to check." Paulo's heart thumped. "Um... maybe she didn't say it." "Thank you for telling me," said Kaito-sensei. "Let's do the sheet together now. It's only five sums." Paulo sat down, cheeks pink, and picked up his pencil.

qa.q: How many sums were on the sheet?
qa.a: It was only five sums.

qa.q: How did Paulo feel after he said his mummy told him not to do it?
qa.a: He felt clever at first, then scared and nervous, with sweaty hands and a thumping heart.

qa.q: What did Kaito-sensei do that helped Paulo learn honesty?
qa.a: Kaito-sensei stayed calm and gently said there would be a check, then thanked Paulo for the truth and helped him with the sheet.

qa.q: How might Paulo's mummy feel if she heard about this?
qa.a: She might be surprised and a little amused, and glad the teacher handled it kindly.

grounding: A young boy lies to his teacher about homework, feels clever and scared, and the teacher calmly checks and thanks him for the truth.

passage: In the classroom at St. Mary's, Thomas Sir walked along the rows checking colouring homework. Rashmi's page was blank. "My mummy said I need not do it," she said quickly. She felt a little smart. Then her tummy went tight. Thomas Sir did not frown. "All right. I'll write in your diary to ask her." Rashmi watched him pick up his pen. "Sir... Mummy didn't say. I wanted to play." Thomas Sir put the pen down. "Thank you for being honest. You can finish it in the break, and I'll help you pick colours."

qa.q: What homework was Thomas Sir checking?
qa.a: He was checking colouring homework.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling as Thomas Sir picked up his pen?
qa.a: She felt scared and uneasy, her tummy tight, worried her lie would be found out.

qa.q: How could a teacher use this moment to build honesty?
qa.a: Like Thomas Sir, they could stay calm, check gently and thank the child for telling the truth.

qa.q: How does Thomas Sir see Rashmi's lie?
qa.a: He sees it as a small childish attempt to play instead, not a big crime, so he responds calmly.

grounding: A young girl claims her mother excused her from homework, feels smart and scared, and the teacher calmly checks and thanks her for honesty.

passage:
Note from the Rainbow room teacher.
Today Madhav and Charu played snakes and ladders. When Charu went to get water, Madhav quickly moved his counter up a ladder. He was giggling and bouncing, but kept looking at the door. Charu came back and said, "That's not where you were!" I sat with them. I didn't say "cheater". I said, "A game is only fun if it's fair. Where were you really?" Madhav moved it back. Then he let Charu roll first. They finished the game laughing. Winning matters a lot at this age.

qa.q: When did Madhav move his counter?
qa.a: He moved it up a ladder when Charu went to get water.

qa.q: What does Madhav looking at the door suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt excited about winning but also a bit guilty and worried about being caught.

qa.q: Why did the teacher avoid the word "cheater"?
qa.a: Calling him a cheater could shame him; saying a game is only fun if fair helped him fix it and keep playing.

qa.q: How might Charu feel when Madhav lets her roll first?
qa.a: Charu may feel the game is fair again and happy to keep playing with Madhav. 🙂

grounding: A young boy moves his counter to win, feels excited and guilty, and a teacher reminds him a game is only fun if fair.

passage: In the mango grove, it was Avni's turn to count. "One, two, three..." She peeked between her fingers and saw Simran run behind the haystack. She giggled into her hands. "...ten! Ready or not!" She ran straight to the haystack. "Found you!" Simran frowned. "You peeked!" Avni's cheeks went hot. Nani was sitting on the charpai shelling peas. "Avni," she called, not cross. "The game is only fun if it's fair. Want to count again with your eyes shut?" Avni covered her eyes properly. This time it took her ages to find Simran, and she loved it.

qa.q: Where did Simran hide?
qa.a: Simran ran behind the haystack.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when Simran said "You peeked!"?
qa.a: She felt guilty and embarrassed, her cheeks going hot, after the excitement of finding her so fast.

qa.q: What did Nani do that helped?
qa.a: She calmly said the game is only fun if it's fair and offered a fresh count, without calling Avni a cheater.

qa.q: How might Simran feel when Avni counts again properly?
qa.a: Simran probably feels things are fair again and enjoys hiding without being spotted straight away.

grounding: A young girl peeks during hide and seek, feels excited and guilty, and her grandmother says the game is only fun if fair.

passage: The power went out halfway through the game, so Yogesh and Tarun played carrom by torchlight. Tarun's Mummy said the bus was coming in ten minutes. Yogesh ran to get water. When he came back, Tarun's striker was right by the pocket and a black coin was in. Yogesh's face went hot. "Cheater! You moved it!" Tarun shrugged. "Did not." Yogesh stamped. Then he took a breath. "That is not fair. Put it back and play properly." Tarun grinned sheepishly and pulled the coin out. They finished the last round before the bus honked.

qa.q: Why were they playing by torchlight?
qa.a: The power went out halfway through the game.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he shouted "Cheater!"?
qa.a: He felt furious and cheated, his face hot, because Tarun had moved the coin while he was away.

qa.q: What did Yogesh say after he took a breath, and why was it better?
qa.a: He said it was not fair and asked Tarun to put it back and play properly, which fixed the game instead of ending it.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel when Yogesh asks him to play properly?
qa.a: Tarun likely feels caught and a little sheepish, but relieved Yogesh still wants to play.

grounding: A young boy catches his friend cheating, shouts cheater in anger, then asks him to play again properly.

passage: On the balcony of their building, Thomas and Chinmay were racing toy cars on a chalk track. When Thomas turned to wave at a pigeon, Chinmay pushed his own car right up to the finish line. "I win!" Thomas spun round. "Cheater! You pushed it!" He was so angry he threw his car. Then he picked it up again. "That's not fair. Let's play again properly." Chinmay did it again the next race. Thomas put his car in his pocket. "I'm going to play with my puzzles. Bye." He walked inside, still cross but calmer.

qa.q: What were Thomas and Chinmay racing?
qa.a: They were racing toy cars on a chalk track.

qa.q: How was Thomas feeling when he threw his car?
qa.a: He was furious and felt cheated after Chinmay pushed his car to the finish line.

qa.q: Why was walking away a fine choice the second time?
qa.a: Chinmay kept cheating after Thomas asked to play properly, so leaving protected Thomas without a fight.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel when Thomas walks inside?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and a little lonely, realising cheating spoiled the game for both of them.

grounding: A young boy calls out his friend for cheating, asks to play again properly, and walks away when it happens again.

passage:
Coach's note for Rafiq's parents, after sports day practice.
Rafiq and Hemant raced three times. Rafiq wanted to win so much that he started before I said "go", twice. The second time he looked back at Hemant and laughed, but his eyes were worried. Hemant said, "Not fair!" I called both back. I told Rafiq, "You can be proud if you try your best, whatever happens." On the third try he waited for "go". Hemant won by a step. Rafiq stamped once, then ran over and gave Hemant a high five.

qa.q: How many times did Rafiq start before "go"?
qa.a: He started before "go" twice.

qa.q: Why might Rafiq's eyes look worried while he laughed?
qa.a: He wanted to win badly, but part of him felt uneasy and guilty about breaking the rule.

qa.q: What did the coach say that could help Rafiq next time?
qa.a: The coach said he can be proud if he tries his best whatever happens, which moves the focus from winning to effort.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel after the high five?
qa.a: Hemant may feel happy about winning fairly and respected by Rafiq.

grounding: A young boy starts early to beat his classmate, and a coach helps him see pride in trying his best.

passage: The school ground in the kasba was dusty and loud. Jahnavi and Afreen crouched at the chalk line for the sack race. Jahnavi wanted to beat Afreen more than anything. Before the teacher shouted "go", she jumped. The whistle blew. "Jahnavi, come back." Jahnavi's face burned. The teacher, Sunita Ma'am, bent down. "I know you want to win. You can be proud if you try your best, whatever happens." On the restart, Jahnavi waited for "go". Afreen beat her by a hop. Jahnavi fell over laughing and still felt proud.

qa.q: What race were Jahnavi and Afreen in?
qa.a: They were in the sack race.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when the whistle blew?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, her face burning, after starting early because she wanted to win so badly.

qa.q: Which part of Sunita Ma'am's response helped Jahnavi?
qa.a: She named Jahnavi's wish to win and told her she can be proud of her best effort, so Jahnavi waited properly.

qa.q: What is it like for Afreen when Jahnavi starts early?
qa.a: Afreen may feel it is unfair and upset at first, then pleased to win the fair restart. 😊

grounding: A young girl starts early to beat her rival, and a teacher helps her find pride in trying her best.
